The post AI is raising the first rung: Who will turn graduates into professionals? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
Join HEPI, AHEP and TechnologyOne for a webinar on Thursday 12 November, 12pm-1pm, exploring the findings of The invisible majority (HEPI Report 205), a study of the professional and support staff who make up more than half of the UK higher education workforce. The session will examine the impact of financial pressures and organisational change on these staff, and discuss how universities can protect the skills and capability they depend on while budgets remain tight. Find details of speakers and register here.

This blog was kindly authored by Professor Mohamed Abdel-Maguid, Pro Vice-Chancellor for Education, Student growth and Global Engagement at Canterbury Christ Church University.

The debate about Artificial Intelligence (AI) and graduate jobs is usually framed as a question of job numbers: how many entry-level roles will disappear? This matters, but in my view, it is not the most important question. A deeper risk is that artificial intelligence is absorbing the work through which graduates develop into trusted professionals.

Routine analysis, first drafts, basic coding, first-triage casework, standard research and reporting were never the most exciting parts of professional life. But they did two jobs simultaneously. They created value for the employer and gave junior staff repetitive tasks, feedback, supervised responsibility and space to make bounded mistakes. This was a form of apprenticeship, even when nobody called it so.

For decades, there was an implicit arrangement: Universities developed disciplinary knowledge, skills and initial competences; Employers recruited graduates and carried part of the cost of turning graduate competences into trusted professional judgement and, where relevant, professional bodies set the standards. Over time, the graduate transformed from a novice with foundational capabilities to a professional trusted to act independently and exercise judgement when faced with new and unfamiliar situations.

Artificial intelligence disrupts this implicit arrangement.

The Institute of Student Employers’ Student Development Survey 2026, which draws on responses from 144 employers, reports that 87 per cent of employers expect artificial intelligence to reshape graduate and apprentice roles. Forty-three per cent say their entry-level roles have already evolved in response to it but have not been formally redesigned.

PwC’s 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer provides clear evidence of what is happening. Its analysis of 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the United States found that most AI-exposed junior roles are seven times more likely than the least AI-exposed roles to require capabilities traditionally associated with more senior staff. These ‘seniorised’ roles that require leadership, judgement and adaptability from junior staff have grown by 35 per cent since 2019, while non-seniorised roles have declined by 10 per cent. PwC reaches a similar conclusion about the development problem: as AI absorbs routine work, some of the activity that once served as an informal apprenticeship is disappearing.

Evidence from the UK Institute of Student Employers (ISE) points to a similar story. ISE’s Student Recruitment Survey 2025 found that graduate hiring had fallen by 8 per cent year-on-year, with competition reaching a historic high of 140 applications per vacancy.

This is not just a simple story of disappearing jobs. The first rung of the professional ladder is being raised. Employers are asking for judgement, leadership and adaptability earlier, while reducing the routine work through which those capabilities were traditionally developed. We are asking graduates to walk into their first jobs with experience before giving them the space to develop it.

Who now owns graduate professional formation?

Universities cannot solve this by adding an artificial intelligence module to every course; nor should they claim the responsibility for the whole of professional formation. Employers and professional bodies remain essential. But the implicit arrangement between them is beginning to break down. Universities cannot safely assume that employers will continue to provide the same developmental bridge between graduate competences and professional judgement.

Three decisions are now needed:

First, universities should define what graduate-level judgement means in each discipline and design for it across the whole student learning journey. Judgement is not something we can assess in separate modules and hope it will somehow accumulate into professional capability. Students need repeated opportunities to work with unfamiliar problems, incomplete or conflicting evidence and consequences. They also need ample opportunities to use AI, challenge it and explain why they accepted, modified or rejected its outputs. A polished output or a working artefact is no longer sufficient evidence of capability.

Second, employers should consider not only the productivity value of junior work but also its developmental value before fully automating it. This is not an argument for preserving inefficient tasks or workflows. It is an argument for replacing their implicit apprenticeship function in a deliberate way through supervised projects, simulation, exposure to clients and progressively greater decision authority. Otherwise, there is a risk that optimising today’s workflows will weaken tomorrow’s pipeline of expertise.

Third, government should use the newly established Early Careers Jobs Alliance to develop a ‘graduate formation model’ for AI-exposed sectors. Universities, colleges, employers, professional bodies and Skills England should work together to establish who develops which capabilities, where that development happens, and who pays for it. Funding for placements, degree apprenticeships and employer-led training should then support this model, with access and success monitored by socioeconomic background.

The equity point is important because if professional formation moves out of paid junior work and into mainly unpaid internships, and other routes dependent on additional credentials, graduates from disadvantaged backgrounds will face a first rung that has moved well beyond their reach.

On the positive side, AI may create more interesting and productive entry-level roles. However, we still need a credible route from novice to trusted professional.

title: Goldsmiths fine art students call for compensation over record tutor strike
summary:

Students arriving at Goldsmiths, University of London this autumn found a campus embroiled in a bitter industrial dispute that has upended timetables and disrupted courses.

“I was really excited to start my studies at Goldsmiths,” one international student told the Guardian at a gathering of unhappy students on Friday. “But when I first arrived, I was quite shocked because almost all the induction sessions seemed to turn into discussions about strikes.”

The international student was one of the unlucky ones, having enrolled on the master of fine art (MFA) course that has been among the worst affected, with 10 out of the 12 usual tutors on strike, and students now saying they want compensation from the university for their lost learning.

Florence Sweeney, a part-time student, said there had been “virtually no teaching” so far this term for many of the fine arts students, and that a group were seeking remuneration.

“Not only has it been a financial drain, but I can see my cohort are very distressed and anxious, and some are depressed by what’s going on,” Sweeney said.

“Some people have moved from the other side of the world, and for them it’s such a risk. To not even get welcomed or proper briefings, it’s really disappointing, especially for a place with such a good reputation for producing exceptional contemporary artists.”

Goldsmiths is famous for the stellar array of artists among its former students, including Steve McQueen, Sarah Lucas and Damien Hirst. But it has been financially squeezed in recent years by falling applications in its core humanities subjects and the erosion of domestic tuition fees, setting off what one staff member described as “non-stop” rounds of redundancies and restructuring.

Now entering its 21st week and with no end in sight, the current strike involving University and College Union (UCU) staff is the longest in living memory in British higher education, originating from a staff marking boycott in April over proposed job cuts.

Goldsmiths’ management responded firmly to the boycott by deducting 100% of pay from those involved. The union argued that amounted to a lockout and a formal ballot followed, so that since early June a group of UCU members at the south-east London university have been on indefinite strike.

Joe Newman, a Goldsmiths UCU branch co-president, said: “We’ve resisted as much as we can over the last two rounds of restructuring and redundancies. But right now, the scale of the action that we are taking is in response to the unprecedented scale and speed of the cuts management are pursuing.”

Newman said students were largely supportive because they “have more in common with staff on precarious contracts than with senior managers on six-figure salaries”, who he said wanted more savings despite earlier cuts.

“When we talk to the students about why we are on strike, of course there are a range of opinions, but overwhelmingly they are just aghast,” Newman said. “The students who have been here longer have seen the impact of previous cuts and seen how things have only got worse. Students who are new can’t believe that management is about to launch an incredibly messy redundancy process.”

The university said only “a small portion of our staff – around 8.5%” were on strike, leaving most students unaffected, and that it had offered significant compromises to the union, including a pause on compulsory redundancies. But it was not prepared to scrap the 100% pay deductions for the marking boycott, saying it had spent significant amounts to ease the impact on students.

“Like many UK higher education institutions, Goldsmiths faces significant financial challenges, which need to be addressed to ensure its future sustainability,” a spokesperson for the university said.

“We recognise colleagues’ right to take industrial action, but continued disruption risks further impacting students’ education and the university’s hard-earned reputation as a world-renowned academic institution in the long-term.

“We are doing everything we can to monitor and mitigate disruption, and are supporting students on courses affected by this strike action, including offering students’ regular updates, meetings with their schools and other appropriate support as needed.”

MFA students said they had been disappointed by the impact on the two-year course, which charges nearly £15,000 a year for full-time UK students and £33,000 for international students.

John Carver, a part-time student in his second year, said he had decided to suspend his studies after attending a “dismal” departmental meeting at the start of term.

“I’m a mature student, time matters to me, and I would be going into a chaotic situation where tutors have been on strike for so long. There wasn’t any light at the end of the tunnel,” Carver said.

“The tutors at Goldsmiths are fantastic, and the way they interact in tutorials, when you do get them, it’s as good as it gets, you build relationships with all the tutors. But what’s going on now is that [replacement] tutors are being brought in who don’t know the students and it’s not as impressive, to put it politely.”

James Evans, an international student from the US, said visa and funding restrictions meant he had to stick with the MFA course despite the disruption.

“Towards the end of last year, in the first days of the strike, I never received marks back, the end-of-term show wasn’t graded. The marks aren’t the important part, but the dialogue is, and there were very important fixtures for the year that went without any discussion. It was a bit frustrating. But this year it’s been worse,” Evans said.

“Our fees went up this year, [and] as an international student they were exorbitant to begin with. There’s still no feedback on projects from last year, but beyond that there’s no structure, barely any communication. We’ve been left to our own devices. It’s been difficult to navigate.”

title: Higher training costs for older workers risks plan to tackle youth jobs crisis, employers say
summary:
Exclusive: Ministers planning overhaul of apprenticeship funding to increase cost of over-25s training, Guardian understands

Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing businesses to pay more to train older workers risks damaging its goal to tackle the youth jobs crisis.

The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training a worker over the age of 25 in England by 25%, to encourage firms to train young people instead.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Britain’s largest employers have told the government that forcing businesses to pay more to train older workers risks damaging its goal to tackle the youth jobs crisis.

The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’s apprenticeship funding scheme to increase the cost of training a worker over the age of 25 in England by 25%, to encourage firms to train young people instead.

Drawn up before Wednesday’s budget, the proposal, which was first reported last week, is expected to form part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are unemployed.

The chancellor, John Healey, is widely tipped to announce measures to bolster opportunities for young people to help the 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training (Neet) across the country.

However, business leaders urged the government to reconsider the plan to make training older workers more expensive.

“It will just mean opportunities are shifted around instead of creating new ones,” said Robert Halfon, a former Conservative skills minister who is now the executive director of policy at the manufacturing lobby group Make UK.

“We agree that getting young people back into employment and training is a moral and economic imperative. But making it more expensive for employers to train older workers isn’t the answer,” he added.

Calling on Healey to “break the cycle” of cutting and reallocating the apprenticeship budget in England, Halfon said the system was already struggling to deliver what businesses and young people need.

“If the government is serious about getting young people into good jobs and giving industry the skills it needs, it should use that opportunity to grow the number of apprenticeships available rather than restrict training elsewhere.”

Andy Burnham has placed youth jobs at the heart of his agenda, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and plans to reverse a 40% drop in youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.

With over-25s accounting for more than half of new apprenticeship enrolments, ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the system towards supporting more younger people.

Under the latest proposal, which is yet to be finalised, employers would be able to fund the full cost of an apprentice under the age of 25 using the money they contribute to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn-a-year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system.

However, for an older worker, they would face a “co-investment rule” whereby levy funds would cover 75% of the costs. The rest would need to be covered separately.

Employers have for years been told they were free to spend their levy funds on training as they saw fit.

John Foster, the chief policy and campaigns officer at the CBI lobby group, said: “We can’t make skills a zero-sum game.

“While it is right to focus on supporting young people who are Neet into work, adult training also has a vital role to play in opening up entry-level opportunities and helping people adapt and update their skills mid-career, particularly as AI reshapes the workplace.”

Ben Rowland, the chief executive of the Association of Employment and Learning Providers, said: “The key to any further changes to the apprenticeship system is to bring employers on the journey. Anything that is too abrupt or too quick significantly endangers that.”

Business leaders have been pressing Healey to use Wednesday’s budget to provide support with soaring costs amid the war in the Middle East, and have urged the chancellor not to add to the pressure on firms after Labour’s increase in employer national insurance contributions.

Kate Shoesmith, the director of policy and insights at the British Chambers of Commerce, said: “At a time when businesses are under pressure to improve productivity and drive growth, employers need greater flexibility and support to invest in skills at every stage of a person’s career.

“The best way to encourage more youth apprenticeships is to make it easier and more affordable for firms to take on young people by reducing the wider costs of doing business, rather than creating new barriers to training.”

Labour has been told its youth skills strategy risks failure without reform, after just 160 young people were enrolled into its foundation apprenticeship scheme in the first eight months. Ministers have an ambition for 30,000 starts over the current parliament.

Joe Dromey, the general secretary of the Fabian Society, said that while flexibility was important for business, the current system was skewed too heavily towards funding older, often already highly qualified workers.

“These will not be easy decisions, and some will be unpopular with businesses. But tackling youth unemployment means making difficult choices about where public funding is spent.”

A government spokesperson said: “It’s right that we focus on reversing the 40% decline in the number of young people starting an apprenticeship and give them the skills they need to succeed.

“That’s why we have reformed the system backed by £3.3bn to deliver 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people and support employers with a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16- to 24-year-old apprentice.

“The Milburn Review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”

title: When community colleges close, rural students get shut out of the liberal arts
summary:
Last May, just weeks before the end of the semester, students, staff and faculty at the University of Wisconsin—Platteville Baraboo Sauk County received the devastating news that the school was closing. Students scrambled to arrange transfers to other colleges, while employees tried to line up jobs elsewhere in the UW system.  By the end of […]

The post When community colleges close, rural students get shut out of the liberal arts  appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Last May, just weeks before the end of the semester, students, staff and faculty at the University of Wisconsin—Platteville Baraboo Sauk County received the devastating news that the school was closing. Students scrambled to arrange transfers to other colleges, while employees tried to line up jobs elsewhere in the UW system.

By the end of the month, “Boo U,” as it was affectionately named, a fixture in south-central Wisconsin for nearly 60 years, was no more.

The Baraboo campus was just the latest UW school to close its doors. In the past three years, the University of Wisconsin has permanently shuttered eight of its 13 branch campuses. With their focus on the liberal arts, these two-year transfer colleges long provided an accessible, affordable on-ramp to higher education, especially for rural and first-generation college students.

To mark Boo U’s closing, instructors and students held a celebration to pay tribute to the college. Among the guests: members of the very first graduating class, who received their associate degrees in the 1970s, two years after the school opened.

“It was really a memorial,” says Karen DeSanto, a first-term Wisconsin state legislator who represents Baraboo. “The students talked about how this place shaped and changed lives in this community. We don’t have that any more.”

In recent years the pace of colleges shutting down has ticked up. According to analysis by The Hechinger Report, colleges are now closing at a rate equivalent to nearly one every three weeks. And yet within this trend, the demise of Wisconsin’s two-year public colleges remains something of an outlier. The other colleges that have closed or are at risk of closing are overwhelmingly private institutions.

University of Wisconsin officials have cited steep declines in enrollment to justify the closure of the campuses. While the UW system has seen enrollment drop by more than 10 percent since 2010, the decline has been especially acute at the two-year schools. In its final year of operation, Boo U had just 100 students, down from more than 500 just a decade ago. Plunging student numbers meant that revenue was no longer enough to keep up with facility, staff and infrastructure costs.

But a shortage of students is only part of the story. Years of budget cuts, beginning under former Republican Gov. Scott Walker in 2015, in concert with a series of tuition freezes, have left the UW system among the worst funded in the nation.

Then in 2017, UW approved a sweeping merger, making the two-year colleges regional branches of the state’s four-year schools. This set off a competitive scramble for students that pitted the two-year UW schools against bigger, and better resourced institutions, some of which lowered admissions requirements to lure more students.

“At that point the writing was really on the wall,” says Dan Kallgren, who spent his career teaching history at UW-Marinette, outside of Green Bay.

Marinette ended in-person instruction in 2024, then limped along for another year offering remote classes. Kallgren taught the final course at the school: a Western Civilization survey class, beamed out via video link to students in Manitowoc and Sheboygan. “I was the last faculty member on campus,” recalls Kallgren.

UW officials insist that even with the shuttering of the rural campuses, Wisconsin students still have plenty of options to choose from, including 13 four-year schools across the state and 16 technical colleges.

But Kallgren says that argument fails to acknowledge the unique role that liberal arts schools like Marinette have played in letting rural students effectively try out college.

“Think about the rural kid screwing up his courage and coming here, then getting turned on to engineering or history,” says Kallgren. “That avenue is now closed.”

Education deserts

Despite the popular notion of students venturing far away to attend college, most students enroll at a campus within 20 miles of home. That’s according to extensive research by scholar Nicholas Hillman, who formerly directed a research lab at UW-Madison and is now an education professor at Indiana University. Hillman found that proximity to a college is associated with higher levels of postsecondary enrollment.

But the inverse is also true. As distance grows between a student and a school, the odds of them enrolling drops. Hillman calls regions with fewer colleges and universities “education deserts,” and warns that Wisconsin is pursuing the higher education equivalent of “desertification.”

“They’ve hollowed out the two-year schools and the liberal arts transfer mission and now they’re sealing the coffin,” says Hillman. “The question is, if you shut one door, have you opened another?”

That doors are closing for Wisconsin’s rural students appears to be borne out by data. Previous reporting on college access in rural communities found that the number of rural students enrolled in the UW system has dropped at a rate greater than the overall decrease in college attendance. While the decline has many causes, including a political backlash against higher education in the state’s conservative rural regions, the shuttering of the branch campuses is likely to exacerbate that trend.

The winnowing of college options in states like Wisconsin reflects a larger story about institutions that serve low-income and rural students closing or being starved of resources.

“People don’t realize the contrast between schools where programs are being cut and (UW-)Madison where the world is your oyster,” says Douglas Haynes, a professor of English at UW-Oshkosh and the author of “Teaching Toward Slow Hope: Place-Based Learning in College and Beyond,” a new book on higher education in the upper Midwest. “There are going to be increasing numbers of (rural) students who just don’t go to college any more.”

A recent study found that Wisconsin has the second highest rate of “brain drain” in the country, as young, educated workers move out of the state after graduating. Haynes says that diminishing college access creates another form of brain drain in which young rural Wisconsinites are deprived of opportunities at the front end. “When we limit college access we’re also limiting the kind of impact these students might have had in their own communities,” says Haynes.

The Wisconsin Idea

Alex Stevens grew up in Stevenson, Michigan, a small town on the Upper Peninsula. Unlike many of his high school classmates, Stevens always knew that he wanted to attend college, but with a disabled mother, both distance and cost were major concerns.

“I was raised by my grandparents, and I knew that caring for my mother was going to become my responsibility,” says Stevens. He would end up choosing the nearest college option, 25 miles down the road and over the state line in Wisconsin: UW-Marinette. “It just made sense to go there.”

He thrived at the school with its small campus and intimate class sizes. Stevens’ favorite courses were sweeping interdisciplinary examinations of U.S. history taught by professors of history, music and film.

After two years, and with almost no college debt, Stevens transferred to UW-Green Bay to pursue a history degree. He now teaches history and social studies at a Catholic high school in Marinette.

“I was rural, poor, and smart and UWM gave me a remarkable opportunity,” says Stevens.

Today, Stevens’ trajectory is much less likely, and not just because the Marinette campus is gone. Wisconsin has also steadily moved away from the liberal arts emphasis that was at the core of the mission of the two-year transfer schools.

In 2023, Jay Rothman, who served as president of the University of Wisconsin before he was fired in April of this year, set off a firestorm with his recommendation that colleges in the system shift from liberal arts programs to more career specific programs, “particularly if the institution serves a large number of low-income students.”

An investigation by student journalists at UW-Madison found that of 82 academic programs within the UW system that have been cut or eliminated in recent years, the majority were in the humanities or social sciences.

“There is an increasingly narrow focus on vocational education,” says Alyssa Ratledge, who studies rural higher education issues at MDRC, a nonprofit research group. She says that closure of the branch campuses and the elimination of majors reflect a broader shift in how states like Wisconsin view the purpose of higher education.

“It’s all about getting a job with a positive ROI (return-on-investment),” says Ratledge. “But students also go to college to try things out and discover who they are.”

As the branch campuses disappear, the expansive notion of higher-education-for-all known as the Wisconsin Idea — the Progressive-era vision that education should improve people’s lives outside the classroom — is also in retreat. In Baraboo, the community is now debating what to do with a cluster of empty buildings.

In Marinette, the theater arts program is the only one remaining, thanks to a partnership with UW Green-Bay, private donations and event ticket sales. Lauryn Albaugh is in charge, and she’s hopeful that the programming, including community and children’s theater, will inspire young people here as it did when she was growing up in Marinette.

Cast in “Willy Wonka Jr.” at the age of 7, Albaugh has never looked back.

“I really attribute my love for the arts to this theater program,” she says. “That it’s thriving feels very encouraging.”

Still, today Albaugh is one of just two employees left at UW-Marinette — a maintenance man inspects the mothballed facilities once a week.

Jennifer C. Berkshire is the host of the education podcast “Have You Heard” and the co-author (with Jack Schneider) of The Education Wars: A Citizen’s Guide and Defense Manual. She teaches in the Boston College Prison Education Program and the Education Studies program at Yale.

This story was originally published by Barn Raiser.

This reporting is part of a collaboration with the Institute for Nonprofit News‘ Rural News Network. Five nonprofit newsrooms were involved: Barn Raiser, Carolina Public Press, Mountain State Spotlight, Oklahoma Watch and Shasta Scout. The series was edited by veteran investigative editor Dee J. Hall, co-founder and former managing editor of Wisconsin Watch. Support from Ascendium Education Group made this project possible.

title: Why Students Hesitate to Seek Campus Support
summary:
Why Students Hesitate to Seek Campus Support
Joshua.Bay Mon, 10/26/2026 - 03:00 AM

New research from TimelyCare examines why students hesitate to seek support and how colleges can make the first step toward getting help easier.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Colleges and universities have long provided a range of support services to help students navigate academic, financial and personal challenges, but just because those resources are available doesn’t necessarily mean students will use them. A new report from TimelyCare finds that many students face barriers to seeking support, even when they know where to find it.

The report draws on an online survey conducted by College Pulse in August and September of more than 1,500 college and high school students, including nearly 1,200 undergraduates at two- and four-year institutions. The research examines how students move from recognizing personal challenges to deciding whether to seek help, identifying the disconnect between awareness of available resources and their use as the “activation gap.”

While 92 percent of college students knew their institution offered at least one of eight types of support, only 59 percent reported using one or more. The services surveyed included academic, basic needs and health care resources.

Seli Fakorzi, director of mental health and client liaison at TimelyCare, said the findings highlight the need to make accessing support easier for students.

“What we’re seeing is that there needs to be an easy on-ramp, an easy first step,” Fakorzi said. “Something that is going to allow them to understand what they need next. But that entry point has to be the simplest first step.”

Barriers to support: The survey found that students aren’t always forthcoming about their struggles. Some 68 percent of undergraduates reported telling someone they were fine or OK when they weren’t during the previous 30 days. Only 35 percent said they would answer a private digital check-in from their institution honestly.

Reaching out proactively to students, including at high-pressure periods in their journey, can be effective in engaging students in care, Fakorzi said. “Not just waiting for them to raise their hand for help—because we know that that’s going to be a hurdle for them early on.”

Taking the first step toward support can itself be a barrier. Some 46 percent of undergraduates identified not knowing where to start as a moderate or major barrier, while 45 percent cited the effort required to take that first step and 44 percent noted feeling their concerns weren’t serious enough.

Despite these barriers, students expressed interest in more accessible ways to seek support. Some 83 percent agreed that a low-pressure first step would help them decide whether to talk to someone, while 77 percent wanted guidance on when to connect with a professional.

Fakorzi said the barriers students face can vary depending on their circumstances, including their level of education and concerns about privacy. Undergraduate and graduate students, for example, may have different reservations about seeking support, while high schoolers may worry about whether their parents will find out.

“When the risk is low, it’s easier for them to contemplate what those next steps are going to be,” Fakorzi said. “Something like having services available 24-7, making sure that students are able to access care wherever they are and understanding that that low-pressure first step should also be an entry point that helps them decide whether they need additional support is a good place for us to investigate what those easier on-ramps are.”

The findings also point to potential implications for student persistence. More than one in five undergraduates had seriously considered stopping out, transferring or leaving their institution during the previous six months. That figure rose to 24 percent among students who described themselves as doing OK or getting by, compared with 12 percent among those who said they were thriving.

“There could be fear, there could be just a lack of knowledge on health literacy and education of mental health resources,” Fakorzi said. “But that tells us that even if they’re saying they’re OK but considering not returning next semester, there’s something missing there.”

Making support accessible: Fakorzi acknowledged that campus health and support professionals are often balancing multiple responsibilities while working with limited resources, making it challenging to ensure students can access the help they need.

Ultimately, Fakorzi said, the findings underscore the importance of understanding what prevents students from seeking support and creating more accessible avenues to appropriate care.

“One of the biggest things for us is just understanding how the gap shows up for our students,” Fakorzi said. “Giving students a frictionless first step, connecting them to human coaching, licensed care or crisis support—this is the conversation for that.”

“How do we easily get them to that point and then also ensure that it’s proactive engagement? That’s something we can start as soon as possible,” she added.

title: Why has France struggled to address students’ demands?
summary: Protesters demand more spending on education and social services, but the government has struggled amid a fiscal crisis.
full_text:
Young people in France continued their nationwide protests over the weekend, demanding better education facilities and a promising future amid the rising cost of living in the country.

France’s Ministry of Interior said 410,000 people protested nationwide on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris, as the government has struggled to address the issues raised by the student-led protests.
