France was also roiled by nearly two years of protests beginning in 2018 over the high cost of living and opposition to French President Emmanuel Macron’s economic policies. Those protests, which were led by the Yellow Vests movement, demanded that the government address the rising economic inequality, boost welfare and public services, and tax the rich.

As the young protesters take to the streets, many of the old demands remain unfulfilled. So, why have French politicians been unable to address the issues facing the country?

Here’s what we know:

Why are young people in France protesting now?

The youth-led protests in France erupted last month amid deteriorating conditions in schools, broader economic anxieties and opposition to government budget cuts.

The protests began in mid-September after high school students blockaded campuses over overcrowded classrooms (often 32–35 pupils per room), unreplaced teacher absences, and dilapidated building infrastructure.

Protesters have waved placards reading statements like “We have a future to build, not to endure”, as they expressed frustration with shrinking public resources and state investment.

Teachers have also joined the students protesting over low salaries. French teachers are paid less on average than their counterparts in other European countries like Germany, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Education at a Glance 2026 report.

School teachers in France earn a gross salary of 41,968 euros ($46,900) per annum compared with 69,453 euros ($77,700) for their German counterparts. Social taxes, high pension contributions and the rising cost of living eat into their monthly income.

What started as a localised strike over school resources has since drawn in trade unions as well as civil servants, and the protests have evolved into a broader economic and political crisis.

This is due to discontent over the government’s proposed 54-billion-euro ($60bn) package of cost-cutting and tax measures for the 2027 budget, which includes civil servant salary freezes.

Students and youth fear bearing the brunt of public spending reductions amid a multidecade high in poverty rates and rising costs of living, exacerbated by the United States-Israel war on Iran.

Currently, according to Amine Snoussi, a journalist for Le Media TV and a former parliamentary assistant at the French National Assembly, the condition of public high schools is dire since government money is being spent elsewhere.

“Students are studying in cold, dirty buildings, some of them infested with rats. In some schools, absent teachers haven’t been replaced for over six months. And all of this is happening while thousands of teaching jobs are being cut, and while public money keeps flowing to private schools. That’s what lit the fuse,” he told Al Jazeera.

What has been the government’s response?

The French government has responded to the mass protests by imposing curfews and deploying police across the country to crack down on protesters.

President Macron has blamed ultra-left groups for trying to “bring down the Republic” and threatened accountability for those involved in violence.

On Friday, the French leader met representatives of the student movement for the first time since the protests began.

But the meeting failed to defuse tensions, with student representatives calling for further mobilisation until the government presents concrete actions.

On Monday, during a visit to Marseille, Macron said he has “asked the government to address the legitimate demands at the root of this protest movement”.

The government is also expected to announce changes to Parcoursup, France’s national online university admissions platform, according to French media reports.

Why is the French government struggling to address protesters’ demands?

Analysts say the French government is struggling to address students’ demands due to a severe fiscal crisis and planned budget cuts, which have led to a drop in the country’s education budget.

According to data published by French economist and co-director of the World Inequality Lab Lucas Chancel, “The public budget for higher education, student life, and research (relative to the total number of students in France, once inflation is taken into account) has decreased by 20 percent since 2017.”

The French government has defended the budget cuts.

In an address to the nation on October 7, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu acknowledged that “the anger among young people didn’t come out of nowhere” and promised the government would present a plan to address the crisis by the end of October.

The French prime minister has also asked his ministers to check spending as France’s national debt has ballooned to about 3.6 trillion euros ($4 trillion), which is equivalent to 119 percent of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP).

Of greater concern to markets than the total debt is France’s growing deficit, however, which is expected to reach 5.4 percent of GDP in 2026 – far above the European Union average of just more than 3 percent. This is the amount by which a government’s spending exceeds its income.

But in a report, French economist and professor Thomas Piketty noted that while public debt has increased, the country’s private wealth has also grown from “300 percent to 600 percent of GDP, with extreme concentration among the wealthiest financial fortunes”.

“In other words, France has never been richer. The problem to solve is simply one of distribution,” he added.

Does France have a wealth distribution problem?

France has relatively low to moderate income inequality, but wealth redistribution has been an issue of debate, particularly in left-wing political groups.

People aged 60 and older, who form a quarter of the population, own 60 percent of the country’s wealth (non-financial and financial), according to a January 2026 review by prominent French economic policy think tank OFCE.

A huge chunk of government funds go to service social security.

A government report seen by the Reuters news agency earlier this month also noted that nearly one-third of some French ministries’ budgets pay for the pensions of retired civil ‌servants, which reduces spending on education and other priorities.

Snoussi told Al Jazeera that the wealth distribution question has always been central to current French politics.

“Macron is called the rich people’s president for a reason. He always supports rich people and has never managed to create a form of equality between classes,” he said.

Macron has been branded “the president of the rich” for cutting the wealth tax. He has also faced criticism for his economic policies aimed at modernising the economy and creating jobs. His decision to impose a fuel tax triggered the 2018 so-called Yellow Vests protests, a grassroots movement seeking government intervention to address inequality.

Critics say his policies resulted in redistribution of wealth upward and affected the working-class population. But Macron has defended his policies, particularly his decision on wealth tax, saying that forcing the wealthy out of the country won’t help the poor.

“I don’t believe in this French jealousy which says, ‘There are rich people; let’s tax them and we will all feel better,’” he told The New York Times in a 2017 interview.

Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at INSEAD in Fontainebleau, France, told Al Jazeera: “France has a more redistributive system than other European countries – at least similar”.

He explained that redistribution is a set of programmes of taxes and transfers that redistribute income from high-income individuals towards lower-income individuals.

The real issue, Fatas said, is deeper.

“France’s growth has been limited for years. With low growth, it is not hard to imagine parts of the population that are unhappy with the progress they see, and this leads to demands for a solution in the form of government support or redistribution,” he said.

France is currently facing significant fiscal stress, with its annual budget deficit forecast at 5.4 percent of its GDP, well above the standard European Union ceiling of 3 percent. The country also remains heavily backed by its public sector, with state expenditures consuming roughly 57 percent of its total GDP – including a notable 14 percent allocated strictly towards worker pensions.

“The assumption is that someone out there is rich enough that they can be taxed. While I can imagine in a more progressive system in France, one has to be careful about the limitations of these apparent solutions,” Fatas added.

So how should the government respond?

In his opinion column for the French newspaper Le Monde, Piketty wrote that reinvesting in sectors like education and health should be the government’s priority.

“Reinvesting in these sectors today is not simply a matter of equality between regions or social classes,” he wrote, highlighting that such reinvestment would help an economy produce greater output by using fewer resources.

Snoussi shared a similar view.

“The government has a simple choice: invest, or step aside,” he said.

“But the real question is whether Macron even wants a way out. Or is he hoping the situation gets worse, so he can crush the movement through police and judicial repression?”

Fatas, the economics professor, noted that while there are a lot of good things people in France want the government to do, it is important to prioritise which sector requires funding.

“The government spending [in France] is the largest among advanced economies, so there is little room to just spend the way out of this.

“France faces a political paralysis when it comes to reform decisions, and this is the reason why they are in a more difficult situation than others,” he added.

title: English, AI and employability: the triple test facing international students
summary:
International students are being asked to master English, get to grips with AI and prepare for a fast-changing job market. Helping them is a job for the whole sector, writes Pearson’s Shileen Costain.

The post English, AI and employability: the triple test facing international students appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Picture an international student, six weeks into her first term in Manchester. Her English is better than she thinks, but the seminars move fast, and last Thursday she used an AI tool to summarize the lecturer’s handout.

She read the university’s AI guidance in week one and she still isn’t sure whether she’s within policy, and she’d rather not ask in case it sounds like a confession. Her lecturer tells her every employer will expect her to use these tools. English, AI, the world of work: she is being asked to get to grips with a lot, a long way from home.

Anyone working in international education will probably recognise her.

Start with English. For an international student it has always been the first hurdle, and it is just as important in today’s AI-enabled landscape. In Pearson and AWS’s AI Readiness research, half of employers put communication and collaboration among their top three requirements for graduates, more than any other skill. International students will also need the judgement to question and check what AI produces – which will demand a high level of English proficiency.

Then there’s AI itself. Most students are finding their own tools. About half use independent tools for writing, against 20% who use their university’s, and only 34% are highly confident they’re following the rules. In the UK, students are better informed about guidance than anywhere else we surveyed, yet just 35% are comfortable telling staff about all their AI use. That looks like a question of trust, and trust takes time, especially in a new country.

Amongst all this, trust in higher education remains strong. Nearly two thirds of respondents (63%) say AI makes a university education more essential, not less. Yet only 14% of learners say their university training has developed their ability to apply AI tools to a professional workflow to a high level, while employers identify limited hands-on experience with workplace AI tools as a leading barrier to graduate readiness.

Experience is hard to build alone. UCL’s Industry Exchange Network, run by its engineering and computer science departments, offers one answer. It hands students live problems from employers, around 1,500 projects a year, and 40 to 45% of participants are later recruited by their industry partners.

It starts with the real-world English they need, not just to pass a test, but to analyse complex content, take part in a seminar and critically evaluate a textbook

So, what helps? International students need support built around them. It starts with the real-world English they need, not just to pass a test, but to analyse complex content, take part in a seminar and critically evaluate a textbook. Without it, it’s all too easy to reach for an AI assistant to translate on the spot and, in doing so, outsource the learning.

Universities can help by setting clear guidance on AI, so that hidden use doesn’t open a trust gap and push the use of AI underground. They also need to give lecturers direction on how AI can be used responsibly in the workplace, so it can be incorporated into their teaching.

Employers can set out what “ready” to work with AI looks like, role by role, rather than in general terms. The judgement a legal assistant needs to decide when to override an AI tool is not the same as the judgement a pharmacy technician needs to understand a dispensing workflow.

None of this needs inventing. Much of it is already underway. What’s missing is the connection between policymakers, universities, employers and those of us who assess learning. Until we make it, international students may be left to work it out alone, six weeks into a new course in a new country.

title: Australian universities back new benchmark for education agents
summary:
Six major Australian education providers have joined a new initiative aiming to put student feedback at the heart of how education agents are evaluated and provide stronger evidence of their contribution to international education.

The post Australian universities back new benchmark for education agents appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Edith Cowan University, Griffith University, Monash University, Navitas, UNSW Sydney and the University of Sydney have signed on as inaugural partners of miXagent, a benchmarking initiative developed by the team behind miXabroad.

The project will gather independent, comparable feedback from international students about their experiences with agents, covering the journey from their initial decision to study overseas through to enrolment and arrival.

“Education agents make an enormous contribution to international education, and we need better evidence to demonstrate that value to governments, policymakers and the broader community,” said Emily O’Callaghan, CEO and co-founder of miXabroad.

“By bringing the student voice into that conversation, we can move beyond anecdotes and build a much stronger understanding of the impact agents have on students’ decision-making, preparedness and early experiences.”

According to miXabroad, education agents play a “vital role” in international education, connecting students with study opportunities, helping them navigate complex decisions and supporting their transition to studying in another country.

Yet, the organisation said that “despite their significant contribution to international education, there remains limited independent, comparable evidence capturing how students experience and value the advice and support they receive”.

“When students start their international education journey, it’s one of the biggest decisions of their lives,” said O’Callaghan.

Education agents are often critical in supporting students through this early stage of their journey, helping them navigate a range of complexities

Emily O’Callaghan, miXabroad

“Education agents are often critical in supporting students through this early stage of their journey, helping them navigate a range of complexities.

“With miXagent, we’re creating an opportunity to better understand what quality support looks like and where improvements are needed.”

The initiative comes amid an increased focus across international education on agent governance, ethical recruitment and demonstrating quality.

miXagent has been developed in consultation with institutions and industry experts, including an advisory council with expertise spanning agent quality, governance and student experience.

It has also drawn on input from individuals involved in the International Education Association of Australia’s (IEAA) Agent Quality Research Project.

“There has been significant work across the sector to strengthen agent quality and governance,” said O’Callaghan.

“We see miXagent as adding another important piece to that picture: a consistent, independent measure of how students themselves experience the advice and support they receive.”

For participating institutions, the ambition is not only to identify problems, but to recognise agents delivering strong student experiences and establish benchmarks that can be shared across the sector.

Jon Chew, chief insights officer at Navitas, said agents’ influence can begin well before a student reaches campus.

“The advice, guidance and reassurance they provide can have a lasting impact on a student’s confidence and experience,” he said.

“We’re excited about the opportunity miXagent provides to better understand those experiences, celebrate the great work happening across our agent network, and work collaboratively with our partners to identify and share best practice.”

At the University of Sydney, director international Tim Field said comparable data could help institutions move beyond evaluating agent performance in isolation.

“Strong agent partnerships are built on trust, shared expectations and a commitment to student success,” he said.

“We know many agents are delivering exceptional experiences, and we want to be able to recognise and learn from that.”

Field said hearing directly from students would allow institutions to identify both successful practices and areas for improvement.

“Having access to comparable insights across institutions will also help us lift standards collectively, rather than working in isolation.”

Danielle Hartridge, miXagent advisory council member and co-founder and principal at IES Advisory, said student feedback should become a more fundamental part of agent oversight.

“We cannot genuinely claim to put students at the centre of international education if we are not actively listening to what they tell us,” she said.

“The student voice should not be an afterthought in education agent governance; it should be one of its foundations.”

“miXagent offers an exciting opportunity to make student experience a measurable and meaningful part of how we evaluate quality, accountability and good practice across the sector,” said Hartridge.

title: Proposed new OPT fee would decimate the international talent pipeline
summary:
Zuzana Čeplá Wootson, deputy director of federal policy at the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, argues that proposed OPT fees would harm students, employers and US competitiveness.

The post Proposed new OPT fee would decimate the international talent pipeline appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
On October 7th the Trump administration proposed charging colleges and universities $70,000 before recommending an international student for Optional Practical Training, or OPT, and $30,000 for subsequent recommendations.

OPT allows students to apply their education in the workplace through temporary professional training and experiences directly related to their field of study. These fees would put that opportunity beyond reach for most students, institutions, and employers.

If implemented, the rule would harm not only international students and campuses, but also domestic students, employers, and US global competitiveness. Preventing that harm requires all hands on deck — from higher education and business leaders to local communities and members of Congress.

There is immediate action to take. Institutions, students, employers, and members of the public can submit comments until November 9 documenting the harms to educational opportunities, research projects, administrative functions, and economic contributions the proposal would cause.

The administration claims the change is necessary to prevent fraud, but its own explanation reveals its broader goal: far fewer students participating in OPT — or potentially no program at all. The DHS explicitly states in the text of the rule that the fees would reduce the pool of participants.

It also states that, without these egregiously high “fees” — or tax as some analysts argue — it may shut down OPT entirely. Ultimately ,either path threatens to dismantle a crucial educational opportunity and talent pipeline.

Any possible case of fraud should be investigated and violations addressed, but this proposal would create a “pay-to-play” system. It would split students into two groups: the few who can participate because they, their employer, or their institutions can afford the fees, and those excluded despite meeting the same eligibility requirements.

DHS argues that the substantial financial stake would encourage schools to exercise greater oversight and selectivity when recommending students for OPT.

Yet the proposed rule ignores existing institutional processes and does not establish how the ability to pay is related to a student’s eligibility to participate in OPT or the value of practical training. Two students could meet the same requirements and have equally valuable opportunities, while only the one whose institution, family, or employer can finance the charge could participate.

Institutions already facing financial pressures cannot simply absorb these costs and DHS can’t assume employers will cover them. Small businesses, startups, arts groups, religious organizations, and other nonprofit employers may have valuable training opportunities to offer without tens of thousands of dollars available to secure a graduate’s participation.

title: 15 Most Elite Colleges in Ohio
summary: Ohio Campuses The ranking is not official but an editorial list using a qualitative index to help determine which schools are considered the “best” universities in Ohio. The ranking weighs the factors of academic distinction, areas of specialization and documented advanced learning opportunities for undergraduates. Elite does not necessarily mean the most selective schools but […]
full_text:
The ranking is not official but an editorial list using a qualitative index to help determine which schools are considered the “best” universities in Ohio.

The ranking weighs the factors of academic distinction, areas of specialization and documented advanced learning opportunities for undergraduates.

Elite does not necessarily mean the most selective schools but rather those considered to have excellent academics that provide the best learning opportunities. This list should not be interpreted as designating the best Ohio university for any particular major.

Depending on your goals (conservatory for music, co-op engineering programs, research opportunities at a liberal arts college, etc.) your list of top schools may vary. Ohio is home to many highly regarded four-year institutions including liberal arts colleges known for close interaction with faculty, a major music conservatory, and universities with co-op programs that combine an academic degree with on-the-job professional experience.

15

Bowling Green State University

The Honors College provides an environment for those seeking an especially challenging curriculum. Students can enjoy the benefits of a large public university while being part of a close-knit group.1

Another opportunity that isn’t exclusive to Honors students is the Center for Undergraduate Research and Scholarship, which encourages students from all majors to engage in research, creative, or scholarly projects in close collaboration with a faculty mentor. Contrary to what many people believe, such work isn’t limited to students studying the sciences; plenty of opportunities also exist in the arts, humanities, and social sciences.2

BGSU provides plenty of exclusive opportunities without excluding other students, demonstrating the difference between exclusivity within a university and exclusivity that is university-wide. If you know what you want to study and are interested in finding a mentor to guide you along the way, Bowling Green offers a wide range of opportunities for you to explore.

Independent work is highly encouraged, but students gradually take on more responsibility as their abilities grow. Come to Bowling Green with a plan!

14

Kent State University

Kent State University has a bit of everything.3

Kent State’s honors program offers many of the same intimate experiences found at a small liberal arts college, but within the context of a large research university.4

And Kent State’s specialty focus in fashion dovetails nicely with this notion: the School of Fashion Design and Merchandising has its own unique curricula and requirements, offering a distinct pathway within the Kent State experience. Kent State ranks among Ohio’s best schools in part because of programs like these.

When choosing a school, it’s not just about the name on the diploma, and sometimes it’s more important to look at the classes that lead up to that degree.

For Kent State’s fashion program, that might be a combination of studio, design, business, or merchandising courses.

For students interested in other disciplines, the calculus is the same. Kent State is a great example of how programs with specialized emphases can succeed within a research university dedicated to providing an education for the masses.

13

Xavier University

For students looking for a rigorous, integrated undergraduate education in the liberal arts and sciences that’s informed by ethical and religious reflection, the Core Curriculum at Xavier University offers an argument that’s stronger than one based simply on the selectivity with which Xavier admits students.5

The Core Curriculum reflects Xavier’s Catholic, Jesuit identity by bringing together the best elements of the liberal arts with the university’s emphasis on faith and ethics.6

The goal of the Core Curriculum isn’t simply to help Xavier students acquire knowledge for its own sake; it’s also to challenge students to reflect on how that knowledge can and should influence their decisions and their responsibilities to others.

Beyond the Core Curriculum, Xavier offers students numerous ways to pursue intellectual interests, including, notably, direct lines to faculty that enable Xavier undergrads to undertake creative projects and original research. By building relationships with Xavier professors through coursework in their academic departments, Xavier students can take interests they’ve developed in class and build on them through sustained, substantive projects.

All of this adds up to a coherent approach to undergraduate education that gives Xavier students a strong, shared foundation while encouraging them to pursue their individual interests with ever-increasing depth and sophistication.

And for students looking to integrate their faith with their education, Xavier’s religious ethos provides another reason to attend a university whose appeal isn’t defined simply by its prestige.

12

John Carroll University

John Carroll’s Integrative Core calls for courses from across departments to be interrelated with one another and with language, humanities, social science, and natural science.7

Not just for general education, either. The core spills over into the major, which must include a capstone experience, other writing-intensive coursework, and an oral presentation component.8

Those are only a handful of the ways this University Heights school demands that its students synthesize and apply what they’ve learned, rather than simply checking boxes.

It’s this type of breadth-plus-synthesis that earns this Jesuit-inflected liberal arts college its spot on the list, bolstered by a host of resources for undergrads looking to stay on track through their degree.

11

Ohio Wesleyan University

Wondering what you might not know that you should know? Ohio Wesleyan University’s OWU Connection is an applied learning program that could help answer that question.9

Known for bringing together research, global learning, service and career exploration into one program, Delaware, Ohio-based OWU has developed a cohesive, integrated program that directly connects theory to practice.10

The OWU Connection offers several options, including signature projects that enable students to explore more deeply into an area of academic interest through service, creative activities or an internship. Financial support to defray the cost of these experiences may be available.

The best projects challenge your assumptions, ask good questions and expose weaknesses in your knowledge, things that can’t necessarily be accomplished in the classroom alone.

And that’s where OWU’s Connection program really shines: by linking theory and practice. This hands-on approach to education makes OWU an ideal school for students seeking a well-rounded education with real-world applications.

So, which OWU Connection opportunity would allow you to take your learning beyond the classroom and test your abilities in the field?

10

Ohio University

Ohio University has two distinct honors programs, Honors Tutorial College and the OHIO Honors Program.11

They’re not interchangeable and shouldn’t be confused.12

The more unusual of the two is the Honors Tutorial College, which focuses on tutorial-based learning. Honors Tutorial College provides a tutorial-based experience at Ohio University similar to that of a small private college but within the context of a large public institution.

While it’s a strength for Ohio University to have this kind of in-depth option for undergrads, we want to note that not all courses at Ohio University are structured this way, which is why OU ranks below other more broadly focused public schools. Still, the Honors Tutorial College offers an individualized path for those looking to explore a discipline in-depth within the context of a larger university setting (in this case, OU’s Athens campus).

Be sure to check out more about the program, including the application process and what the school looks for in candidates, to get a sense of what a typical day would look like for Honors Tutorial College students.

9

University of Dayton

Research problems don’t come with the answer already worked out. Nor do they always provide a set of clear steps to follow.13

That’s what makes research so challenging and so rewarding. Dayton’s catalog lists experiential learning, including research, as a central part of its undergraduate education model.14

Cooperative education, internships, community-engaged projects and service, creative projects, laboratory and field experiences. All of these experiences allow students to explore connections between their area of study and the world beyond the classroom.

One standout research opportunity is the Summer Undergraduate Research Experience, a ten-week program for qualifying engineering students. Participants receive support and mentoring, not micromanagement, from Dayton faculty or University of Dayton Research Institute professionals.

The program also gives students an introduction to and path toward continued research opportunities.

Dayton’s commitment to combining experiential learning with rigorous academic preparation means Dayton graduates leave campus equipped to tackle real-world problems.

Dayton’s experiential learning model challenges students to step outside their comfort zones in a supportive, structured environment and leaves them well prepared for the messy, rewarding work ahead.

8

University of Cincinnati

It’s the co-op program that truly sets Cincinnati apart.15

Co-ops are much more than summer jobs. They’re carefully planned educational experiences that combine classroom learning with hands-on, paid work experience related to a student’s future career.16

Cincinnati’s co-op program is designed to give students an edge over the competition by allowing them to put their education into practice in a real-world setting. It also gives them an opportunity to bring their questions and newly acquired knowledge back into the classroom – and then back again the next time they hit the co-op circuit.

Take Cincinnati’s engineering program, for example. According to the College of Engineering and Applied Science, students begin alternating between co-op semesters and academic semesters after their sophomore year and complete five different co-op experiences during their tenure at Cincinnati.

(Not all of Cincinnati’s engineering programs follow this pattern, however.)

It’s this type of professional development that sets Cincinnati’s undergrad education apart from the rest of the pack.

For some students, that hands-on component is worth more than attending an even more selective school, as it gives them a practical mastery of their chosen field and an opportunity to dive headfirst into their dream career – and Cincinnati’s co-op program is tailor-made for those students.

7

Miami University

Miami’s Honors College offers an option for students who want an undergraduate experience that combines breadth with direction, preparing them for graduate study and other advanced work. The Honors curriculum includes research-, application-, and student-driven courses and culminates in an Honors Senior Project.17

This provides students with a culminating goal outside the context of individual classes.18

The Undergraduate Research Award Program offers students the opportunity to apply for funding to conduct research with a faculty mentor. The application process itself teaches students about identifying research questions, articulating their approach to addressing those questions, and defending the importance of their proposed projects.

Miami’s ranking reflects the balance it provides between a structured honors experience and research opportunities.

It’s the cumulative nature of the experience that adds academic value for students.

From an introductory honors class and nascent research question, to a mentored research project and culminating independent piece of work, students at Miami can develop an academic and research agenda that evolves over their time at Miami.

This is the argument for Miami beyond its picturesque campus and familiar name.

It’s not just RedHawk spirit, because there’s substance to be gained as well.

Miami students take control of their experiences, transforming curiosity into accomplishments that prepare them for whatever comes next.

6

The College of Wooster

The College of Wooster is known for the rule: Every. Single.19

Student. Completes.20

An. Independent.

Study. Independent Study is the heartbeat of The College of Wooster.

Independent Study is required for each and every student, and serves as each student’s capstone experience. Students might conduct laboratory research, delve deeply into historical analysis, create a body of artistic work, or many other options.

The through-line: engage in rigorous, serious work using the methods and processes of a particular field. And this isn’t a senior-year-only phenomenon, either; preparation begins early and builds over four years.

For example, the Sophomore Research Program matches students with faculty mentors for paid research assistantships.

Students are challenged to make and defend decisions, and receive mentoring and support from faculty, but ultimately it’s the students’ project.

And this is the key to Wooster’s independent research culture, and to its ranking of six on this list: It’s not about massive research expenditures; it’s about expecting, and enabling, students to take on a challenging question, pursue it over time, and create something tangible that demonstrates their abilities.

5

Denison University

Denison combines a strong liberal arts education with real-world application. Courses tie in directly to hands-on experiences in labs, in the field, or through consulting projects.21

The Summer Scholars Research Program gives stipends, housing allowance, and sometimes additional funds to cover the costs of research. This allows students to devote themselves to a research project with a mentor instead of trying to work it into an already-packed course load.22

Granville is the kind of place that makes an intimate yet exciting undergraduate experience possible. Denison makes the top five because of its combination of intellectual intensity with financial support for research.

The best projects at Denison are interdisciplinary in nature, tackling specific questions that require drawing on more than one field or discipline. Denison’s liberal arts education is broad, but not diffuse.

Students seeking intellectual challenges and an environment that will prepare them for life after college, as doers and not just thinkers, should consider applying.

4

Oberlin College and Conservatory

Not many undergraduate programs offer the combination Oberlin does. Ranked fourth among the best colleges in Ohio, Oberlin offers the best of a top liberal arts experience combined with the challenge and focus of a conservatory music program.23

In fact, there are two schools within Oberlin’s College and Conservatory: the College of Arts and Sciences offers a challenging undergraduate liberal arts program in the humanities, social sciences, and natural sciences, and the Oberlin Conservatory offers a demanding pre-professional program for advanced study in music. Students apply separately to each school, and the most famous option, the Double Degree Program, allows students to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree and a Bachelor of Music degree in a demanding but exciting five years of study.24

Students in the Double Degree Program are not just adding on some easy classes to their main Oberlin degree, and they are juggling two full and demanding degree requirements. Few other programs so seamlessly incorporate the challenge of performance and artistic study with the demands of academic research that characterize the nation’s best colleges, making Oberlin a top option for students interested in majoring in music and another discipline—and a rich environment even for those who aren’t.

3

Kenyon College

Smaller colleges aren’t necessarily known for research, but that doesn’t mean students can’t be actively involved in projects outside of the classroom.25

Research isn’t just for students in lab coats – Kenyon College also encourages science-writing as a way to combine research with effective communication.26

And, for international studies students, the capstone experience isn’t a quickie term paper – it’s a twenty-to-thirty-page independent research project, working closely with a faculty mentor to pull together everything learned in previous courses into one, cogent, well-supported argument. There are also collaborative research projects between faculty and students during the summer, and other research opportunities across disciplines.

All of this research and the high expectations for learning – students leave having developed research questions, worked closely with faculty mentors, and constructed well-supported arguments – goes to show that it isn’t necessarily Kenyon’s intimate environment that earns the College its third-place ranking. Rather, it’s likely due to an index that favors the depth of undergraduate learning, as demonstrated through rigorous capstones, liberal-arts education, and research opportunities – both during and outside of the academic year.

2

The Ohio State University

One of the nation’s premier research universities, The Ohio State University provides students with extensive resources for research in their field of study. These resources include research centers and institutes in a wide variety of fields.27

Students who conduct research culminating in an approved thesis can earn Research Distinction or Honors Research Distinction upon graduation, depending on specific degree program requirements.28

As one of the country’s largest research universities, Ohio State offers opportunities for students to get involved in research in a variety of capacities and to tailor their research experiences to best fit their interests and academic goals. Though there are a multitude of opportunities to get involved in research at Ohio State, there isn’t just one way to do it.

Students interested in research at Ohio State must do the work to find the opportunities that are right for them, and take advantage of the many resources available to craft their own research experiences at Ohio State. For students interested in research, this can mean developing a challenging curriculum in their intended field while still having access to a wide range of other disciplines and areas of expertise.

Ohio State’s impressive resources make it possible for students to chart their own courses, and have support at every turn to help them succeed in their chosen paths.

1

Case Western Reserve University

Case Western Reserve University earns our top ranking not as an all-around academic powerhouse, but as a uniquely research-oriented institution with excellent hands-on opportunities for its students.29

Case Western Reserve University’s Undergraduate Research Office is a great resource for students interested in creative and scientific research who want to take their education beyond just learning what’s already been discovered. The seven-story, 50,000-square-foot Sears thinkbox is also more than just a makerspace; it is an innovation center with resources and programming geared toward entrepreneurship and new venture development.30

Importantly, both resources transcend departmental silos and encourage interdisciplinary collaboration among students with diverse skills and expertise.

For students interested in bridging the gap between theory and application whether by making, tinkering, experimenting, or otherwise taking knowledge beyond the realm of the abstract, Case Western Reserve University has resources and support that are second to none. As such, the university earns the number one spot in our editorial roundup of Ohio’s best colleges, rounding out our countdown with its emphasis on cutting-edge research, hands-on learning opportunities, and resources for undergrads.

title: America’s Highly Selective Colleges
summary: Stanford Campus Some colleges in the U.S. are so exclusive that they accept fewer than one in 20 applicants! From famous research universities to small liberal arts schools and even a music conservatory, the admissions process at these schools can be difficult. These are the 25 toughest colleges to get into in the U.S.! To […]
full_text:
Some colleges in the U.S. are so exclusive that they accept fewer than one in 20 applicants! From famous research universities to small liberal arts schools and even a music conservatory, the admissions process at these schools can be difficult. These are the 25 toughest colleges to get into in the U.S.!

To create this list, we ranked colleges based on their undergraduate acceptance rate for first-time students entering in the fall of 2024.

We limited our list to established schools (graduate-only schools were not eligible), schools that offer bachelor’s degrees and nonprofit institutions. We also required that schools have at least 100 applicants and 100 students.

Overall, acceptance rates aren’t a good indication of your odds of getting in. That’s because not all applicants use the same admissions pathway and schools’ applicant pools differ. We used fall 2024 first-time undergraduate admission data from the National Center for Education Statistics’ 2025 Data Feedback Reports to make this list.

We determined admission rates by dividing the number of admits by the number of applicants.

Then we ranked the schools from the lowest admission rate (calculated with unrounded numbers) to the highest and rounded admission rates to two decimal places. These are historical admission rates, not admission rates for this year.

25

Cornell University: 8.76 Percent Admitted

Cornell University’s overall acceptance rate for fall 2024 was 8.76 percent.1 According to the NCES, there were 62,993 applicants for 5,516 admission offers.1 Cornell University has multiple undergraduate colleges and schools in Ithaca, New York, so prospective students must apply to their intended college or school.2

Engineering students, for example, apply separately from art students.

24

Williams College: 8.25 Percent Admitted

Williams College, a liberal arts college in Williamstown, Massachusetts, offers a distinctive undergraduate experience, with a small learning environment that contrasts with the atmosphere of a large urban research university. Williams College’s tutorial system pairs a professor with two students, cultivating independent work, active participation, and close reading and discussion.4

Williams’ 8.25 percent acceptance rate (1,272 admitted students out of 15,411 applications for fall 2024) shows that even small colleges can be extremely selective.3 Students should enter Williams’ tutorial system prepared to participate, rather than simply listen to lectures.

23

Rice University: 8.00 Percent Admitted

Of the 32,473 applicants for fall 2024, NCES records show that 2,597 students were admitted for an acceptance rate of 8.00 percent.5

However, acceptance rate is only a small part of the Rice story and does not tell prospective students very much about what the Rice experience is like on any given day. Rice is a research university in Houston that also features a residential college system.6

Upon arrival, Rice undergraduates join one of these colleges and remain members throughout their undergraduate career. This system creates smaller communities within the larger Rice community.

22

Northwestern University: 7.69 Percent Admitted

With 3,806 admitted students out of 49,474 applicants for fall 2024 (according to NCES data), Northwestern’s acceptance rate is 7.69 percent.7

Northwestern has six undergraduate schools, so the programs offered range from liberal arts to engineering to communication, journalism, music, and education-related study.8 Northwestern’s overall acceptance rate doesn’t differentiate between its schools and programs.

Students should research their intended program, particularly any additional application requirements.

21

Swarthmore College: 7.46 Percent Admitted

Pennsylvania’s Swarthmore College has an acceptance rate of just 7.46 percent, on par with some of the country’s largest universities.9

According to the National Center for Education Statistics, for fall 2024, the school admitted just 975 students from 13,065 applicants.9 The honors program at Swarthmore is known for its academic rigor, testing a student’s ability to thrive in an environment with high expectations.

For example, in Swarthmore’s classics program, students are tested by external examiners, not just their professors.10

20

Bowdoin College: 7.13 Percent Admitted

According to the National Center for Education Statistics, 946 students were admitted to Bowdoin College out of 13,265 who applied for fall 2024 admission.11

That acceptance rate of 7.13 percent makes it one of the hardest colleges to get into in the USA.11 Beyond its acceptance rate, Bowdoin College in Brunswick, Maine, offers an undergraduate program that encourages exploration, but still has requirements.

Students participate in a first-year writing seminar and must take courses in distribution areas meant to encourage different modes of thought and inquiry.12 In other words, students are still given some leeway, but are encouraged to venture out of their comfort zone. Prospective students should consider this.

19

Colby College: 7.09 Percent Admitted

Located in Waterville, Maine, Colby College is focused on undergraduate education.

Its DavisConnects advising model integrates internships, research, global experiences, and funding.1314 For the fall 2024 academic year, NCES reported that 1,360 of 19,187 applicants were admitted to Colby College, giving it an acceptance rate of 7.09 percent.13

18

Pomona College: 7.09 Percent Admitted

For fall 2024, Pomona admitted just 868 students from a pool of 12,249 applicants for admission, resulting in an acceptance rate of 7.09 percent, according to NCES.15 The two schools round to the same acceptance rate, but Pomona’s unrounded acceptance rate is lower. Pomona’s Claremont Colleges membership adds another layer to its undergraduate experience.16

While still small and close-knit, Pomona students can take courses at other Claremont Colleges thanks to cross-registration, made easy by coordinated registration and academic calendars.16

17

Johns Hopkins University: 6.44 Percent Admitted

Johns Hopkins University, a research university in Baltimore, Maryland, allows students to participate in research as early as their first undergraduate year.18 Applying to Johns Hopkins University is highly competitive, with an acceptance rate of only 6.44 percent.17

For fall 2024, there were 45,895 applicants and only 2,954 were accepted into the undergraduate program, according to NCES.17 This statistic refers to the overall competitiveness of gaining admission to Johns Hopkins University as part of the entering class, not a specific student’s admission chances.17 These statistics do not reflect admission to graduate or professional programs.

16

Vanderbilt University: 5.86 Percent Admitted

Vanderbilt offers the Immersion Vanderbilt program.20

Through Immersion Vanderbilt, students connect experiences outside of the classroom to a culminating project, linking practice with academic work.1920 According to the NCES, Vanderbilt’s acceptance rate for fall 2024 was 5.86 percent.19

Out of 45,409 applications for fall 2024, only 2,662 were accepted to Vanderbilt University in Nashville.

15

Duke University: 5.71 Percent Admitted

With an acceptance rate of just 5.71 percent, Duke University in Durham, North Carolina, is highly selective.21

According to the NCES, there were 2,957 admitted students out of 51,795 applications for fall 2024.21 Programs like Bass Connections are a big part of what makes Duke stand out, bringing together undergraduates, graduate students, and faculty on research teams working to solve complex problems.22

This type of research structure, where students can work together across levels and areas of expertise, can appeal beyond prestige. Those who are interested in collaborative research can explore the various projects and examine the skills they develop. Still, given how competitive admissions are at Duke, the strongest applicants should also explore other options.

14

Dartmouth College: 5.40 Percent Admitted

Another Ivy League school with a similarly low acceptance rate is Dartmouth College.

For fall 2024, NCES data indicates that out of 31,656 applicants, just 1,710 were offered admission, amounting to an acceptance rate of 5.40 percent.23 Penn’s acceptance rate also rounds to 5.40 percent.23

This gap cannot predict individual admission chances.23 Dartmouth offers opportunities including its D-Plan, which gives students control over their academic calendar.24 Within certain parameters, students using D-Plan can choose their enrollment terms and when to step away from academics.24

13

University of Pennsylvania: 5.40 Percent Admitted

Penn has a highly selective admissions process and its 5.40 percent overall acceptance rate reflects that fact.25

NCES data shows that for fall 2024, Penn accepted 3,523 out of 65,226 students who applied to attend the school.25 However, it’s important to note that each of Penn’s undergraduate schools, the College of Arts and Sciences, School of Engineering and Applied Science, School of Nursing and the Wharton School, may differ in selectivity, so this number isn’t indicative of acceptance rates for each school.2526

When applying to Penn, applicants are encouraged to apply to the school that best matches their academic interests and preparation, so prospective students should know their intended school before trying to figure out how selective Penn is.

12

Brown University: 5.39 Percent Admitted

Located in Providence, Rhode Island, Brown University has an acceptance rate of 5.39 percent, and for fall 2024 only 2,638 students were admitted from nearly 49,000 applications.27

Brown University offers an Open Curriculum. The Open Curriculum gives students the freedom to create their own educational journey without a prescribed core curriculum.28

With the Open Curriculum, students still need to demonstrate progress toward a degree and create a coherent academic path.

11

Northeastern University: 5.22 Percent Admitted

With an acceptance rate of 5.22 percent, admission to Northeastern University is highly competitive.29

According to the NCES, there were 98,425 applicants vying for just 5,133 admits for fall 2024.29 This number describes the reporting institution’s fall cohort.

Always check the details of an admission offer, including the location, timing, and conditions of admission, because these details shape your experience.30

10

Princeton University: 4.62 Percent Admitted

Getting into Princeton University is only the first challenge.

With a 4.62 percent acceptance rate, admission is competitive.31 For fall 2024, there were 40,468 applicants and just 1,868 admits, according to NCES.31

The undergraduate experience is centered on independent work, and junior and senior research in particular distinguish this college experience.32 Requirements vary by department, but generally, this work includes formulating a question, overseeing a project that addresses it, and defending a thesis. For this reason, students should focus on much more than acceptance when considering Princeton.

9

Curtis Institute of Music: 4.58 Percent Admitted

One of the most selective programs is the Curtis Institute of Music, which had an acceptance rate of just 4.58 percent for fall 2024.33

According to NCES data, only 26 out of 568 students who applied for fall 2024 admission were admitted.33 Because Curtis is a specialized music institution, all applicants must go through an audition process for admission, and their academic preparation helps determine in which educational program they will be placed.34

While this does make it one of the most difficult schools to get into, keep in mind that the acceptance rate can fluctuate quite a bit when the incoming class is so small. These students sought advanced training in music through a process that assesses artistic talent. Curtis offers full-tuition scholarships to all of its students.34

8

Massachusetts Institute of Technology: 4.55 Percent Admitted

The acceptance rate to MIT is extremely low, meaning that only a small fraction of those who apply get in.

For the fall 2024 entry year, there were 28,232 total applicants and 1,284 admits, according to NCES data.35 That means the acceptance rate is 4.55 percent, showing how competitive admission is.35

MIT’s dedication to research is evident in its Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program, which enables students in all majors and class years, even first-years, to get involved in research projects.36 For those interested in science and hands-on learning, the research opportunities in Cambridge, Massachusetts, are especially appealing.

7

University of Chicago: 4.48 Percent Admitted

UChicago is a research university known for its Core, a program of undergraduate courses that requires students to grapple with important questions across a range of fields and develop their skills of critical inquiry.38

This gives every student in the College, regardless of major, a common core of ideas and experiences to draw from.37 With an acceptance rate of 4.48 percent, the University of Chicago is competitive.37

According to NCES data, UChicago accepted just 1,955 students from a pool of 43,612 applicants for fall 2024.37

6

Columbia University: 3.99 Percent Admitted

For fall 2024, NCES data shows that of the 60,115 people who applied to Columbia University, only 2,400 were admitted, resulting in an acceptance rate of just 3.99 percent.39

It’s important to note that undergraduate pathways at Columbia University include Columbia College and Columbia Engineering. These programs have different admissions processes from the General Studies program.40

The location and academic programs at Columbia University attract many students, but admissions vary by the undergraduate program you’re applying to. This countdown includes application and acceptance data at the institution level from federal reporting to NCES for consistency.39 Other profiles that focus on the specific undergraduate programs at Columbia University may include different data, so keep populations separate.

5

Yale University: 3.87 Percent Admitted

NCES data shows that only 2,227 students were admitted for fall 2024 from a pool of 57,517 applicants, for a 3.87 percent admission rate at Yale University.41

Admissions readers at Yale place heavy emphasis on your high school transcript because it shows your drive and performance over time.42 Beyond the numbers themselves, admissions officers consider the context around your transcript, your achievements, the opportunities you’ve had, and the courses you chose to take.

4

Harvard University: 3.65 Percent Admitted

Harvard University’s acceptance rate is extremely low. According to the NCES, there were a total of 54,008 students who applied to attend Harvard in the fall of 2024.43 Only 1,970 of those applicants were accepted, resulting in an acceptance rate of 3.65 percent.43

Harvard is known for its holistic approach to reviewing applications for admission.44

While grades and test scores are important, Harvard considers other factors, too, such as recommendations from teachers and counselors and other portions of the application to get a sense of who the applicant is as a person.44 There’s no exact formula for admission, and a strong academic record does not guarantee acceptance.

This information refers to first-time undergraduate entry, not graduate or professional schools.

3

Stanford University: 3.61 Percent Admitted

For fall 2024, according to NCES, there were 57,326 applicants and only 2,067 admits, yielding a 3.61 percent acceptance rate.45

Harvard and Stanford may have different admissions rates, but those rates are close to one another. This does not mean that admission to one of these universities guarantees admission to the other, however.

As with most elite universities in the US, competition is fierce for a place at Stanford. Stanford uses a holistic application review process.46 Stanford’s admissions guidance emphasizes students’ performance in challenging coursework.46

2

Minerva University: 3.04 Percent Admitted

Minerva has a distinctive admissions process that differs from traditional universities, so while the reported rate measures applicants admitted, the application experience itself is quite different.

Instead of primarily considering essays and a student’s academic record, for example, the Minerva application includes challenges that demonstrate how a student thinks.48 The 3.04 percent acceptance rate is due to Minerva admitting 330 students out of 10,864 applicants in fall 2024, according to NCES records.47

Though Minerva’s acceptance rate is comparable to schools like Harvard and Stanford, it receives far fewer applications than those elite universities.

1

California Institute of Technology: 2.57 Percent Admitted

Caltech has a common core curriculum that all students complete prior to and concurrently with additional coursework in a chosen area of concentration, called an option at Caltech.50

Caltech also has the lowest admission rate here, with an acceptance rate of just 2.57 percent.49 For fall 2024, NCES records show that Caltech accepted 356 students out of 13,856 applicants.49

While there are other highly selective institutions with more applicants than Caltech, Caltech still extended very few admission offers to its applicant pool, making it a reach for many.

title: Podcast: „Die digitale Welt ist durch das Amoklaufen der KI-Konzerne gefährdet“
summary: KI-Professorin Alke Martens warnt vor Weltuntergangserzählungen und sagt, wo die eigentliche Gefahr liegt: In dem, was Sprachmodelle mit unserem Denken machen.
full_text:
Als Alke Martens 2007 an der Universität Rostock Juniorprofessorin wurde, gab man ihr einen klaren Rat: „Wenn du jemals eine Vollprofessur bekommen möchtest, dann lass deine Finger von KI, weil da wird es nichts mehr geben, das ist tot.“ Ihre Professur hieß deshalb „Kognitive Systeme und E-Learning“, das Wort KI vermied man. Heute ist Martens Professorin für praktische Informatik in Rostock und mit mehr als 270.000 Followerinnen und Followern eine der reichweitenstärksten KI-Erklärerinnen im deutschsprachigen Netz. Im c't-Podcast „They Talk Tech“ mit Svea Eckert und Eva Wolfangel erzählt sie, dass sie von einer jungen Mitarbeiterin vor die Kamera geschickt wurde, weil sie sich „ohnehin täglich über KI aufrege.“ Geplant waren 10.000 Follower im ersten Jahr, nach einem halben Jahr waren es knapp 100.000.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Die Resonanz erklärt Martens mit ihrer fachlichen Mischung: Sie hat Informatik mit Nebenfach Medizin studiert und schließlich in der KI über Expertensysteme für das Lehren und Lernen promoviert. In Rostock verantwortet sie die Lehramtsausbildung in Informatik. Dinge so herunterzubrechen, dass sie auch Schulkinder oder IT-ferne Eltern verstehen, sei ihr Handwerk. Umso mehr ärgere sie, wie gut Untergangsszenarien funktionieren. Die Erzählung, KI werde uns alle töten, verdecke ein reales Problem, das nur wenige einschätzen könnten: „KI-Systeme gefährden unsere Infrastruktur“, sagt Martens, „die digitale Welt ist durch das Amoklaufen der KI-Konzerne gefährdet.“

Hinter den Apokalypse-Schlagzeilen vermutet Martens Kalkül. „Das ist eine gezielte Marketing-Strategie.“ Angesprochen würden nicht Nutzerinnen und Nutzer, sondern Investoren, die sich Milliardengewinne versprechen. Dabei sei das Gesamtkonstrukt nüchtern betrachtet absurd: „Das ist eine Software, die auf zusammengeklauten Daten basiert“, sagt Martens, „und die versuchen sie jetzt hochpreisig an die Börse zu bringen.“

Empfohlener redaktioneller Inhalt

Mit Ihrer Zustimmung wird hier ein externer Podcast (Podigee GmbH) geladen.

Martens erklärt im Podcast auch die Basis der Technologie, die an sich nicht neu ist. Die Grundideen stammten aus den 1950er-Jahren. Schon früh gab es zwei Stränge: regelbasierte Expertensysteme, die kaum Fehler machen, aber starr sind, und probabilistische Verfahren, die Häufigkeiten auswerten. Neuronale Netze erkannten Muster in Bildern lange vor dem aktuellen Hype. Ihre Schwäche demonstriert Martens Studierenden mit Hunde- und Katzenfotos: Haben alle Hunde einen schwarzen und alle Katzen einen weißen Hintergrund, lernt das System nicht, Hunde und Katzen zu unterscheiden, sondern eben den Hintergrund. Neu seien vor allem GPUs, die Milliarden gleichförmiger Rechnungen parallel ausführen. Und natürlich die Datenmassen aus dem Netz. „Mit dem aufkommenden Internet 1989 ist eine Harvesting-Maschine entstanden, wie man in den USA sagt“, eine Erntemaschine also: „Wir werden im Internet sozusagen geerntet.“ Wer in Foren wie Reddit oder auf X viel schreibt, bekommt im Modell die größte Stimme – wer dort nicht vorkommt, wie etwa ihre 83-jährige Mutter, gar keine.

Um die Folgen für Menschen geht es in Martens' neuem Buch „Dumm dank KI?“, das sie im Podcast erstmals vorstellt. Menschen passten sich an die Technik an, sagt sie, und zwar auf drei Ebenen: in der Sprache, die KI-Floskeln übernimmt; im Vertrauen auf Antworten, die gut klingen, aber nur Wahrscheinlichkeiten abbilden; und in Schule und Uni, wo bei Prüfungen und Noten oft nur noch das fertige Produkt zähle, nicht der Lernprozess. Den Vergleich mit früheren Technikängsten lässt sie nur begrenzt gelten. „ Der Taschenrechner hat eine extrem hohe Zuverlässigkeit. 2 plus 2 ist beim Taschenrechner immer 4.“ Er habe uns das Rechnen abgenommen, nicht die Mathematik. Bei Sprachmodellen sei das anders: „Das, was uns die KI jetzt wegnimmt, ist die Fähigkeit des eigenen Ausdrucks. Und das ist heikel.“

Ihren Studierenden sagt sie deshalb deutlich, dass sie KI-generierte Arbeiten nicht sehen will. Als Vertreterin einer Bildungseinrichtung wolle sie die jungen Leute verändern: „Ich möchte, dass ihr herausgeht und andere seid, als ihr vorher gewesen seid.“ Sinnvolle Einsatzfelder für KI-Systeme sieht sie eher in schmalen, gezielten Anwendungen wie etwa dem Transkribieren. Dafür brauche es aber keine großen Sprachmodelle. Diese seien weder Therapeut noch Lehrkraft-Ersatz, sondern „schlicht und ergreifend eine Spracherzeugungsmaschine, die auf Wahrscheinlichkeiten basiert“.

„They Talk Tech“ erscheint jeden Mittwoch überall, wo es Podcasts gibt. Svea Eckert und Eva Wolfangel diskutieren ein Tech-Thema oder treffen inspirierende Frauen aus und rund um die Tech-Welt.

full_text:
Un polo da circa 250 milioni di euro di ricavi netti per rafforzare la distribuzione all’ingrosso di libri scolastici e di varia. È il perimetro di XL, la joint venture che nascerà dall’accordo vincolante sottoscritto da EmmeEffe Libri con Mauro Padovani – fondatore di Txt – e la famiglia Portesani di Centro Libri. Quella che va a configurarsi e che Il Sole 24 Ore è in grado di anticipare è un’operazione che mette insieme due specializzazioni: la fornitura di testi scolastici alla grande distribuzione organizzata e il servizio a librerie e cartolibrerie.

Il controllo (51%) sarà di EmmeEffe Libri, partecipata al 70% dal gruppo Messaggerie e al 30% dal gruppo Feltrinelli. A Padovani andrà il 40%, alla famiglia Portesani il restante 9%. XL controllerà il 100% di Txt e di Centro Libri, quest’ultima già controllata al 51% da EmmeEffe Libri. La costituzione della joint venture è subordinata all’autorizzazione dell’Antitrust. I 250 milioni rappresentano il fatturato consolidato previsionale riferito al 2026.

Alla presidenza andrà Alberto Ottieri, presidente e amministratore delegato di Emmelibri, mentre Padovani sarà l’amministratore delegato. Nel consiglio entrerà anche Riccardo Portesani, ad di Centro Libri. «La principale strategia di crescita del Gruppo Messaggerie nel mercato dei libri di varia e di scolastica avviene tramite joint venture con i principali operatori di mercato», sottolinea Ottieri. «La nascita di XL, in partnership con Mauro Padovani, fondatore di Txt, e la famiglia Portesani, fondatrice di Centro Libri, già nostri soci, consolida ulteriormente un settore strategico».

title: Chimica, produzione a -3%: Ue decisiva. Meloni: intervenire sugli Ets
summary: All’assemblea di Federchimica, gli industriali riportano l’attenzione su energia e salute. Il presidente Buzzella: «Ets fardello»
full_text:
Per gli industriali della chimica, la sostenibilità del sistema dovrà senz’altro guidare anche le scelte industriali, ma da questa consapevolezza non può che derivare una visione ampia del concetto di sostenibilità. Negli anni si sono susseguiti numerosi piani che hanno portato verso quel Green deal che ha messo molto in difficoltà l’industria. E anche la recente revisione del sistema degli Ets per la chimica può considerarsi solo un primo passo. «Tra costi diretti e indiretti del sistema ETS, la chimica italiana versa oltre 600 milioni di euro all’anno, destinati a diventare 1,5 miliardi entro il 2030 - ha ricordato Buzzella -. Un paradosso, se pensiamo che mentre l’UE ha ridotto le proprie emissioni al 5,8% sulle emissioni globali, queste sono invece cresciute nel mondo del 60% dal 1990. Nel frattempo, in Europa, solo tra il 2021 e il 2025, gli investimenti in nuova capacità di prodotti chimici sono crollati del 90%. Non è pensabile ridurre le emissioni attraverso la desertificazione industriale. La transizione ecologica deve essere pragmatica, non ideologica».

All’assemblea di Federchimica nel dibattito è stato dato molto spazio al tema dei temi che resta l’energia e a quello della salute, inteso anch’esso in maniera ampia. «La salute umana, animale e vegetale e la qualità degli ecosistemi non sono ambiti separati, bensì parti di un unico sistema dal quale dipendono sicurezza, benessere e qualità dello sviluppo. Questa visione è ben riassunta dal concetto, in continua evoluzione, di “One Health”, nel quale Federchimica si riconosce pienamente - ha spiegato Buzzella -. Il paradigma va oltre la sanità e richiede di considerare insieme prevenzione, ambiente, alimentazione e attività produttive. La chimica, alla base di farmaci per l’uomo e per gli animali, del medicale e della diagnostica, dell’agricoltura e della sicurezza alimentare ed è dunque uno dei principali fattori abilitanti di One Health». All’assemblea hanno partecipato il presidente di Confindustria Emanuele Orsini e il ministro degli Esteri, Antonio Tajani. Orsini ha ripetuto che «oggi senza chimica non si fa nulla». E tra gli industriali c’è molta preoccupazione perché «lato Europa sembra che ci siamo resi conto solo noi italiani di quello che sta succedendo. Sulla battaglia Ets eravamo da soli, sulla chimica siamo da soli, sull’industria di base siamo soli. Avremo un importante incontro con Confindustria Germania e Confindustria Francia, ma quello che stiamo vedendo noi è che loro stanno dando come dato di fatto che abbiamo perso l’industria di base. Non siamo riusciti a cambiare rotta velocemente come gli altri, la reazione di Usa e Cina è stata molto veloce, non come la nostra». Sugli Ets «noi abbiamo portato avanti una posizione. L’Ets valeva 5,8 euro a tonnellata nel 2016, adesso vale 87 euro. Abbiamo già tanti imprenditori che hanno delocalizzato». Sugli Ets, facendo riferimento al prezzo dei permessi di emissione di Co2 nel mercato dell’Unione europea (Eu Ets), Orsini ha spiegato che «allo Stato italiano noi diamo 2,6 miliardi quest’anno», ma «di quei 2,6 miliardi, all’industria non ne possono arrivare solo 600 milioni, devono arrivare tutti i 2,6 miliardi, perché se no non siamo competitivi. Quei soldi dove vanno? Vanno una parte, gran parte degli Stati membri e una parte della Commissione europea. La verità è che noi imprenditori invece di essere aiutati per essere competitivi stiamo mantenendo la Commissione europea per farci la guerra. Questo noi dobbiamo dirlo, quei soldi sono i nostri, devono servire per fare la decarbonizzazione ed essere più competitivi». Pur trattandosi di un sistema non condivisibile alla radice, tuttavia aiuterebbe a far funzionare il meccanismo «una cosa semplice: il certificato deve essere comprato e rivenduto tra imprese. Questo toglierebbe la speculazione e il prezzo tornerebbe a 6-7 euro. Non tornerei indietro su tutto, ma questo andrebbe fatto».

Tajani ha aggiunto che «c’è bisogno di politiche serie che mettano le imprese nelle condizioni di competere a livello globale. L’Europa rischia di essere travolta nella sfida con Usa, Cina, India perché i lacci e lacciuoli bloccano la competitività del sistema, mentre altrove ci sono molte meno regole. Uno dei temi che ci sta più a cuore è quello del Green deal che non va bene così come è stato applicato. Quando noi dobbiamo difendere l’ambiente dobbiamo tenere presente che non ci sono solo piante, fiumi e animali, ma ci sono anche uomini e donne che devono continuare a vivere e produrre, perchè senza lavoro non c’è dignità. Il Green deal così come è non va. Stiamo combattendo una battaglia sugli Ets, non va bene Ets 1 ed Ets 2. L’altro giorno abbiamo ottenuto un primo risultato ma non basta, e stiamo lavorando perché settori come la chimica possano beneficiare delle nuove regole».

All’assemblea di Federchimica sono arrivati anche i messaggi del ministro delle Imprese e del made in Italy, Adolfo Urso e di quello dell’Ambiente, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin. Di quale Europa ci sarebbe bisogno per industria, salute ed energia si è parlato in una tavola rotonda a cui hanno partecipato Ilaria Capua, Professor e senior fellow of global health alla Johns Hopkins University Sais Europe, Davide Tabarelli, Presidente di Nomisma energia e Giulio Terzi di Sant’Agata, presidente della Commissione Politiche Ue del Senato.

E’ quando i ragionamenti sfociano sui temi energetici che diventano più critici. Per Buzzella «siamo ad un bivio cruciale. Serve una politica industriale in due tempi: proteggere la capacità strategica oggi, trasformarla domani. Per farlo la premessa, è una soltanto: energia sicura, disponibile e a costi sostenibili. L’incidenza dei costi energetici sul valore della produzione chimica è passata dal 14% del 2021 al 18% del 2024, e rischia oggi di superare il 23%. Il gas in Europa costa fino a nove volte quello statunitense. Non parliamo solo di margini che si assottigliano, ma di un rischio concreto di fermate produttive, rinvio degli investimenti e delocalizzazione. E chiudere un impianto significa perdere per sempre competenze, occupazione e sovranità tecnologica». Peraltro, anche a voler essere visionari, non è facile perché i due pilastri della transizione green immaginata da Bruxelles, come l’idrogeno verde o la “CO2 capture and utilization”, sono ancora oggi tecnologicamente complessi ed economicamente non sostenibili per essere utilizzati su larga scala. Per questo la transizione deve basarsi sulla neutralità tecnologica, dando traguardi ambientali ragionevoli e lasciando alle imprese la libertà di scegliere le soluzioni più efficienti per raggiungerli.

full_text:
Un recente articolo su Nature dal titolo “La straordinaria ascesa della Cina nel campo della scienza e come cambierà il mondo” discute come il Paese sia sulla buona strada per diventare leader mondiale nel campo della scienza, uno sviluppo che ridisegnerà il progresso tecnologico, l’innovazione e gli equilibri di potere globali.

L’articolo sviluppa soprattutto questi punti:

Una trasformazione costruita in quasi cinquant’anni. Nel 1978 la presenza cinese nelle pubblicazioni scientifiche internazionali era marginale. Oggi il paese è uno dei maggiori protagonisti della ricerca e dell’innovazione, con risultati nelle tecnologie avanzate e nell’esplorazione spaziale.

La ricerca fondamentale diventa una priorità strategica. Il nuovo piano quinquennale prevede di rafforzarla e di aumentare la spesa complessiva in ricerca e sviluppo di almeno il 7% annuo fino al 2030. Gli ambiti prioritari comprendono intelligenza artificiale, tecnologie quantistiche e fusione nucleare.

Le imprese acquistano un ruolo crescente. Università e istituti pubblici hanno storicamente guidato la ricerca cinese. Le politiche per le industrie strategiche emergenti, avviate nel 2010, hanno contribuito ad ampliare la partecipazione delle imprese private. L’articolo presenta DeepSeek come esempio di innovazione imprenditoriale maturata entro questo contesto di sostegno duraturo.

Lo spazio come investimento di lungo periodo. La stazione Tiangong e le missioni lunari illustrano una strategia che collega ricerca, capacità tecnologica e autonomia nazionale, sviluppata attraverso programmi pluridecennali.

La crescita presenta anche fragilità. L’articolo richiama problemi di integrità scientifica, interrogativi sulla regolazione etica della ricerca biomedica e rischi legati al rallentamento economico e alle tensioni geopolitiche.

La Cina ha superato gli Stati Uniti diventando il paese che investe di più in ricerca e sviluppo (R&S) al mondo, se si considera la spesa cinese calcolata in base alla parità di potere d’acquisto (PPA), un parametro che mira a equiparare i costi. Tuttavia, la spesa cinese in R&S è ancora inferiore a quella degli Stati Uniti se si considera il tasso di cambio

L’ascesa scientifica cinese è il risultato di una costruzione istituzionale durata decenni. Come ricostruisce l’articolo, nel 1978 i ricercatori del paese pubblicavano meno di 120 articoli nelle riviste internazionali censite da Scopus, appena lo 0,02% del totale mondiale. In meno di mezzo secolo, la Cina è diventata una delle principali potenze della ricerca, con risultati che spaziano dall’intelligenza artificiale all’esplorazione lunare. Questa trasformazione ha combinato investimenti pubblici, sviluppo delle università e degli istituti di ricerca e crescente partecipazione delle imprese all’innovazione, sostenuta anche dalle politiche per le industrie strategiche emergenti avviate nel 2010. Il nuovo piano quinquennale prevede un aumento della spesa complessiva in ricerca e sviluppo di almeno il 7% annuo fino al 2030 e un rafforzamento della ricerca fondamentale. Il caso cinese mostra così come la capacità di innovare delle imprese possa maturare entro un sistema scientifico sostenuto nel lungo periodo. La rapidità della crescita presenta però anche contraddizioni, fra cui problemi di integrità scientifica e di regolazione etica: la quantità delle risorse e delle pubblicazioni deve accompagnarsi alla qualità delle istituzioni che governano la ricerca

Ο Διευθυντής του Ελληνικού Ιδρύματος Έρευνας και Καινοτομίας (ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ.), Καθηγητής Γιώργος Καρυδάκης, συμμετείχε στο workshop της Ευρωπαϊκής Επιτροπής με τίτλο: «Οι προκλήσεις και το μέλλον της αξιολόγησης ερευνητικών προτάσεων» (“Challenges and future of R&I proposal evaluation”), το οποίο πραγματοποιήθηκε στις Βρυξέλλες, την Παρασκευή 16 Οκτωβρίου 2026. Το workshop αφορούσε στην ανάδειξη κοινών προκλήσεων και την εξέταση προσεγγίσεων που μπορούν να συμβάλλουν στην αντιμετώπιση τους. Στο επίκεντρο των συζητήσεων βρέθηκε η επίδραση της Τεχνητής Νοημοσύνης στο πεδίο της χρηματοδότησης της έρευνας και της καινοτομίας.

Με την ευκαιρία της επίσκεψής του στις Βρυξέλλες, ο κ. Καρυδάκης συναντήθηκε (15-16 Οκτωβρίου 2026) με εκπροσώπους της European University Association (EUA) και του δικτύου The Guild. Επίσης, πραγματοποίησε συναντήσεις με στελέχη της DG CNECT, της DG EAC, της DG REGIO και της DG RTD της Ευρωπαϊκής Επιτροπής, καθώς και του Εκτελεστικού Οργανισμού του Ευρωπαϊκού Συμβουλίου Καινοτομίας και των ΜμΕ (EISMEA). Οι συναντήσεις πραγματοποιήθηκαν με σκοπό την ανταλλαγή απόψεων σχετικά με κοινές προτεραιότητες και τη διερεύνηση πιθανών πεδίων μελλοντικής συνεργασίας.

Ακολούθησε στρογγυλή τράπεζα με τίτλο “Strengthening the Environment for Frontier Research in Greece – From Barriers to Action”, στην οποία συμμετείχε ο Διευθυντής του ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ., κ. Καρυδάκης, μαζί με την Πρόεδρο του Επιστημονικού Συμβουλίου του Ιδρύματος, Καθηγήτρια Γεωργία Ανδρέου, παρουσία του Υφυπουργού Ανάπτυξης, αρμόδιου για θέματα έρευνας και καινοτομίας, κ. Σταύρου Καλαφάτη και εκπροσώπων της Ελληνικής ερευνητικής κοινότητας. Η συζήτηση επικεντρώθηκε στις προκλήσεις που αντιμετωπίζει η έρευνα αιχμής στην Ελλάδα και ευρύτερα αλλά και στους τρόπους αντιμετώπισής τους.

Μέσα από τη συμμετοχή του σε ευρωπαϊκές πρωτοβουλίες για την έρευνα και την καινοτομία, το ΕΛ.ΙΔ.Ε.Κ. επιδιώκει να παραμένει επίκαιρο και να διαμορφώσει στενούς δεσμούς με φορείς και πρωτοβουλίες σε Ευρωπαϊκό επίπεδο.

Σχετικά

ΔΕΛΤΙΟ ΤΥΠΟΥ
